# Mahāsīhanāda Sutta (MN 12 (PTS MN i 68))

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Mahāsīhanāda Sutta* (MN 12; PTS MN i 68) is set in response to the ex-monk Sunakkhatta, who disparages the Buddha by asserting that his teaching lacks superhuman knowledge and was merely formulated through reasoned inquiry to end suffering [SuttaCentral; Appleton 2015; Gildow 2016]. The Buddha refutes this by maintaining that such an assessment is unwitting praise, though warning that anyone who reduces the Tathāgata's insight to mere logical reflection lands in hell [SuttaCentral; Gildow 2016]. To demonstrate his transcendent spiritual attainment, the Buddha expounds his ten powers (*dasabala*), his four intrepidities (*vesārajja*), and eight assemblies, declaring his right to "roar his lion's roar" [Appleton 2015; Ñāṇamoli and Bodhi 1995]. The discourse also introduces the simile of an *ekāyana* path—conveying the sense of a direct path leading in one direction toward a clear pond—to illustrate the course to liberation [Bodhi 2005; Anālayo 2014].
A notable portion of the sutta recounts severe ascetic practices undertaken by the Bodhisatta, including prolonged fasting, nakedness, wearing coarse garments, and either excessive bathing or allowing layers of grime to accumulate [Deleanu 2006; Stanley et al. 2018; Polak 2011]. Because several of these practices are mutually exclusive, early interpretive traditions—such as the *Lomahaṁsa-jātaka* (Ja 94 / Ja I 390)—assign them to the Buddha's distant past lives [Stanley et al. 2018; Anālayo 2017]. Due to these frightening austerities, the text was also widely known across early traditions as the "hair-raising" discourse (*lomahaṁsa* / *romaharṣaṇa*), an epithet preserved in the *Milindapañha*, Pāli commentaries, Chinese translations, and Sanskrit parallels [Anālayo 2017; Polak 2011].
Within the Pāli canon, its formulas of powers and ascetic practices recur in AN 10.21, AN 4.8, AN 6.64, and the *Vibhaṅga* (Vb 16) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus corroborates extensive text reuse between MN 12 and the *Dasakanipāta* (AN 10), *Ñāṇavibhaṅga* (Vb 16), *Chakkanipāta* (AN 6), and *Catukkanipāta* (AN 4), while showing strong cross-language alignments with the Sanskrit *Daśabalasūtra*, the *Arthaviniścayasūtra*, and various Prajñāpāramitā texts [DharmaNexus].
